blocks.text: PART 1: THE HOUSE THAT NO LONGER BELONGED TO ME
I had spent fifteen years believing my wife would always be waiting when I came home.
That belief lasted until the evening I returned from Rome and found seven boxes standing beside our perfectly made bed.
Not sleeping somewhere else. Not visiting a friend. Not taking a few days to punish me for another argument.
Her closet was empty, her bathroom drawers had been cleared, and the familiar scent of her perfume had disappeared from the bedroom.
Everything belonging to me remained exactly where I had left it.
My suits hung in their usual order. My watches sat inside their glass display cases. My shoes were polished and arranged beneath the wardrobe.
Even the black leather travel bag I had taken to Rome was still resting beside the dressing room.
But Isabelle’s side of the closet looked as though she had never lived there.
I stood in the doorway for several seconds, unable to understand what I was seeing.
Seven identical cream-colored boxes had been arranged in a straight line beside the bed. Each had a small handwritten label attached to its lid.
I recognized the gentle curve of her capital letters and the way she always left a little more space between words than necessary.
My attention settled on the seventh box.
DAY SEVEN: I STOPPED LOVING THE VERSION OF YOU I INVENTED IN MY HEAD.
It was ridiculous, really. I had been away for four days, and she had chosen to turn my return into some elaborate emotional performance.
I opened our message conversation and typed.
I watched the screen for several seconds.
I called her a third time, then sent another message.
Isabelle, this isn’t funny. Call me immediately.
It was resting on a small wooden stand beside the boxes. Its screen was illuminated, displaying a single video file.
There was no thumbnail, no description, and no indication of how long the recording lasted.
My fingers stopped just above the screen.

I had negotiated billion-dollar acquisitions without hesitation. I had stood before hostile investors and defended decisions that could have destroyed my company. I had built Laurent Maison from a struggling fashion label into an international luxury empire.
My estimated net worth was $5.9 billion.
Yet I was standing in my own bedroom, afraid to press a button.
For the first time since arriving home, I remembered Camille.
Seven hours earlier, I had been sitting beside her at breakfast in a luxury hotel in Rome.
She was twenty-six, beautiful, ambitious, and one of the most recognizable faces associated with Laurent Maison.
She had never pretended to be indifferent about our future.
That morning, she had been wearing one of my white shirts, her hair falling loosely over her shoulders as she studied me across the breakfast table.
“When are you going to tell Isabelle?” she had asked.
“I’m tired of pretending this is temporary.”
I reached across the table and touched her hand.
Then she smiled without showing any happiness.
I had kissed her forehead and returned to my email.
At the time, I had considered the conversation finished.
Now, standing in the bedroom where Isabelle and I had shared fifteen years of marriage, those words sounded different.
Perhaps I had used them with everyone who expected something from me that I did not feel like giving.
The paper had faded, and the edges were beginning to crumble. I picked them up carefully.
We had been young, broke, and ridiculously optimistic.
I had barely enough money to pay for our accommodation. Isabelle had packed sandwiches because we couldn’t afford to eat in restaurants every evening.
We had spent the journey sitting beside each other, sharing headphones and laughing about things that were not remotely funny.
I remembered telling her that one day I would buy her a first-class ticket to anywhere in the world.
She had looked at me and said, “I don’t need first class. I just need you to keep coming with me.”
I remembered the way she used to look at me.
I remembered how she believed in everything I said.
YOU PROMISED ME WE WOULD NEVER BECOME TOO BUSY TO REMEMBER WHERE WE STARTED.
The second box contained the rental agreement for our first apartment.
It was a tiny place with peeling wallpaper, unreliable heating, and a kitchen so narrow that two people could barely stand inside it together.
The radiator had stopped working, and Isabelle had wrapped herself in two blankets while I worked on sketches at the kitchen table.
Sometimes she fell asleep sitting beside me.
I would cover her with a blanket and return to my designs.
Back then, I thought those nights were proof that we were building something together.
I didn’t realize how long she had continued doing that after I stopped looking back.
Beneath the rental agreement was a photograph.
We were standing outside the apartment building, holding a cardboard box between us.
I looked younger, thinner, and considerably less certain of myself.
I placed the photograph beside the train tickets.
